h1: Becoming a beer category manager at a retailer
title: Becoming a Beer Category Manager | Craft Beer School
desc: What a beer category manager at a retailer does, from range and shelf space to promotions and freshness. It also shows how people move into the role.
teaser: A category manager decides which beers earn a place on the shelf. It is a buying job that rewards people who understand the product.
standfirst: The beer category manager chooses the range, sets the shelf plan and negotiates with suppliers. This guide covers the work, the numbers and how to move into it.
sections:
A category manager owns the performance of one product group inside a retail business. For beer, that means deciding which brands and pack sizes to stock, how much space each gets, how they are priced and when they are promoted. The goal is a range that sells well, turns over quickly and earns a fair margin.

First, a note on what "retailer" means. Alcohol is a state subject in India. The way beer reaches shoppers differs from state to state. Everywhere it is sold only through licensed outlets. Which kinds of shop can hold a licence differs by state, as does whether a supermarket may stock beer at all. Retail may also mean a hotel chain, a duty-free operator or a restaurant group. Check how the rules work where you live, because they shape what a category manager can actually do. Rules change, so read the current notification.

Most of the week is data and conversation. You read sell-through by brand, pack and outlet. You look for what is slow, what is out of stock and what is growing. You meet suppliers, hear their plans and push back on terms. You agree promotions, check they are funded and watch whether they paid back.

  • Range: which beers to add, keep or drop.
  • Space: how many shelf facings and fridge slots each beer gets.
  • Price: where each beer sits against competitors and within the state's pricing rules.
  • Promotion: what runs when and who pays for it.
  • Supply: whether the shelf stays full without piling up old stock.

The planning cycle is annual, with reviews each quarter and small changes in between. Festive periods and the summer peak drive the calendar.
Why beer is a tricky category

Beer is a fresh product. A packaged lager keeps for months, not years. Hoppy beers fade faster. A category manager who treats beer like canned soup will end up with tired stock on the shelf. Look at the date code on every pack you stock.

Cold storage matters too. Beer left warm in a hot warehouse or a shop with no fridge ages quickly. Ask where a beer will be stored and how long it will sit. A slow-selling craft beer in a warm back room is a brand risk for both retailer and brewer.

Craft beer adds another wrinkle. Small brewers have limited volumes and irregular supply. A range that depends on a beer that is out of stock half the month frustrates shoppers. Ask suppliers about batch size and delivery rhythm before you list.

You do not need advanced maths, but you must be comfortable with a handful of measures:

  • Sell-through: units sold divided by units received over a period.
  • Rate of sale: units per outlet per week. It tells you if a beer earns its space.
  • Gross margin: the share of the selling price left after the cost of goods.
  • Days of cover: stock on hand divided by average daily sales. Too many days and beer ages. Too few and the shelf runs empty.

Learn to move between units. A hectolitre is 100 litres, which is about 154 bottles of 650 ml. Suppliers talk in hectolitres and retailers talk in cases. You will be the translator.

Many category managers come from general retail or FMCG and learn beer on the job. The ones who stand out can taste a sample and say whether a new listing is a genuine style or a copy, explain to a buyer why one beer costs more to make than another and spot when a supplier's story does not add up.

That knowledge also helps you talk to shoppers and store staff. A shelf talker that explains a style in one honest line sells more than a long brochure. If the product is new to you, taste widely and write notes. Our guide to the BJCP judge exam shows one route into structured tasting.
How people get into the role

Typical routes include buying or merchandising assistant roles, sales jobs with a drinks company, category analyst positions and supply chain roles. Analytical skill and a head for commercial detail matter more than a particular degree.

Show that you can read a sales report and make a decision from it. Bring an example: how you would rebalance a ten-beer range if two brands were slow and one was always out of stock.

The role sits next to brewery careers. If you want to understand the supplier's side, read about becoming a brewery operations manager or a brewery project manager. You will deal with people in both roles.

Pick a shop you know and list every beer on its shelf with its pack size and price. Group them by style and by price band. Where is the range crowded and where is there a gap? Then decide what you would add or drop and why. Answering that with data is the job in miniature.
faqs: What does a beer category manager do?
They choose the range, set shelf space and price, agree promotions with suppliers and track sales to keep the category healthy.
Do I need to know how beer is made?
Not at the start, but it helps. Understanding freshness, styles and production lead times lets you buy better and challenge suppliers.
Can any retailer in India sell beer?
No. Alcohol is regulated by each state, so what retailers can stock and how they sell it varies. Check the current rules where you work.
Reading sales data, negotiating with suppliers, planning stock and knowing the product well enough to judge a new listing.
